kurz: How the mark lost value by a factor of one trillion in nine years, and what this means today for thinking in terms of tangible assets.

bloecke.md:
On 1 July 1914, one US dollar cost 4.20 marks. On 20 November 1923, it cost 4.2 trillion marks. The factor between the two figures is a one followed by twelve zeros. A value like this describes more than particularly high [[Inflation|inflation]]: it describes the disappearance of a currency.

The beginning lies nine years earlier. With the outbreak of war in 1914, the Reichsbank's obligation to redeem its notes in gold ended. The Reich financed the war almost entirely through debt instead of taxes, namely through war bonds sold to its own public and through short-term Treasury bills that the Reichsbank bought and thereby turned into money. In the end, the defeated enemy was supposed to pay the bill. With defeat in November 1918, this assumption fell away, but the debts remained. By then, the money supply had already multiplied. This was barely visible because price freezes and rationing kept prices in check. In retrospect, this is called hidden inflation, because the price pressure was there; the price index simply did not show it.

bloecke.md:
After 1918, the price freezes were lifted, and the depreciation that had been hidden until then became visible. The London Schedule of Payments of May 1921 set reparations at 132 billion gold marks. They were payable in foreign currency, so the government had to sell marks for other currencies. Every sale pushed down the mark's exchange rate. The falling exchange rate made imports more expensive, more expensive imports drove up domestic prices, and higher prices forced the state to spend more, which it again financed through the printing press. From 1922 onwards, this cycle ran faster and faster.

In January 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr because deliveries had not been made. The Reich government called for passive resistance. It used newly printed money to pay for the wages, compensation payments and lost tax revenue of the industrial region, where work had come to a halt. From then on, the mark practically no longer performed the functions of a currency. The Reichsbank under Rudolf Havenstein did not see itself as the cause. In its view, the economy was suffering from a shortage of money, and the central bank had to meet this need. That the need was growing solely because the printed money was no longer worth anything remained disputed within the central bank's leadership until the very end.

bloecke.titel: The depreciation of the currency in six steps
bloecke.unter: The fundamental decision was made as early as 1914; in 1923 its consequences became visible.

ereignisse.text: Redemption of the mark in gold ends. The war is financed through war bonds and through Treasury bills that the Reichsbank turns into money.
In January, the dollar costs just over 60 marks. In May, the London Schedule of Payments demands 132 billion gold marks, payable in foreign currency.
In January, the dollar costs around 200 marks, and by October already 4,439 marks. A further decline is expected, and this expectation accelerates it.
In January, the Ruhr is occupied, and the state pays for the passive resistance with newly printed money. The dollar rises from 49,000 marks in January to 53 million marks in September.
From 20 November, 1 Rentenmark equals 1 trillion paper marks. Prices stabilise within days, even though the new currency is not convertible.

In August, the gold-backed Reichsmark is approved, and it is in circulation from October. The Rentenmark remains valid alongside it. The highest note ever printed, for 100 trillion marks, has been in circulation since November 1923; a second issue bears the date 15 February 1924.

bloecke.md: A [[Hyperinflation|hyperinflation]] is a problem of confidence; the rising prices are its consequence. It begins when a state permanently finances its current spending through its own central bank. It ends as soon as the state credibly stops doing so, even if no backing returns.

The equation of exchange M × V = P × Y shows why prices rose faster than the money supply in the end. It states that the money supply times the [[Velocity of money|velocity of money]] equals the price level times the quantity of goods. As an identity, the equation always holds, and on its own it is not yet a theory. It gains explanatory power through V. In normal times, V changes only slowly, over a period of years. In 1923, V shot up because all holders of money did the same thing and spent their money immediately. Employees who received their wages in the morning bought whatever they could get by midday. In the end, wages were paid out daily, in some firms twice a day, so that the workforce could go shopping during their break.

Each of these reactions is sensible on its own. Together, they accelerate the depreciation that each individual is trying to escape. Between January and 20 November 1923, the dollar exchange rate rose by a factor of 86 million. Converted to a daily rate, that is around 6.4%, and to a monthly rate, around a six-and-a-half-fold increase.

bloecke.titel: Purchasing power of 100 marks left unspent (as a percentage)
bloecke.unter: Own calculation using the average daily depreciation in the final phase of around 6.4%; after eleven days, half the purchasing power is lost, and after one month just over a seventh is left.

bloecke.md:
A hyperinflation redistributes more wealth than it destroys. The losers were all those who held claims in marks, such as passbook savings accounts, life insurance policies, private pension promises and mortgage certificates, but above all war bonds, which had often been subscribed out of a sense of duty. A middle-class fortune that had meant a carefree old age in 1914 was worth nothing by 1923.

The winners were all those whose debts in marks were matched by a tangible asset. A block of rented flats, a factory or a stock of goods kept its value, while the mortgage on it shrank to an amount that could later be paid off with the equivalent of a meal. The largest debtor was the state itself. By the end of 1923, its entire domestic war debt had in effect been paid off.

The best-known example is Hugo Stinnes, whom contemporaries called the “inflation king”. He used loans to buy up coal mines, shipyards, hotels and newspapers. After his death in 1924, the group fell apart within a few years because, after the stabilisation, the loans had to be serviced in money of stable value again. The profits of the inflation winners were based to a large extent on borrowed money, and the leverage only worked as long as the depreciation continued.

Some of this was later corrected by the courts and by legislation. At the end of 1923, the Reichsgericht (the supreme court of the German Reich) abandoned the principle of “a mark is a mark”, and the Revaluation Act (Aufwertungsgesetz) of 1925 restored private mortgages at roughly a quarter of their former value in gold marks. War bonds received only minor compensation. The Loan Redemption Act (Anleiheablösungsgesetz) of 1925 exchanged them at 2.5% of their face value. Original holders who had acquired them before 1 July 1920 also received drawing rights (Auslosungsrechte), which were to be redeemed within 30 years at five times this amount plus interest. Those who had trusted the state were thus treated worst.

punkte: Debtors with long-term loans in marks, above all the Reich
Owners of production facilities, inventories and land who did not have to sell
Exporters whose costs were incurred in marks and whose revenues came in foreign currency
Anyone who was able to hold foreign currency early and discreetly
Subscribers to war bonds and holders of savings deposits
Life insurance policyholders and recipients of private pensions and annuities
Creditors of every kind, including mortgage lenders
Wage earners whose pay rose more slowly than prices

bloecke.md:
On 15 November 1923, the [[Rentenmark]] was introduced. From 20 November, 1 Rentenmark equalled 1 trillion paper marks. Land charges (Grundschulden) on agriculture, industry and trade served as “backing”. This was a book value that nobody could redeem, because there was no counter at which a Rentenmark could be exchanged for a field. The stabilisation had other causes. The quantity issued was firmly capped in number, the Reich no longer received any credit from the central bank, and in Hjalmar Schacht a currency commissioner took office who visibly kept to this limit. Within a few days, prices stopped rising. Contemporaries spoke of the “miracle of the Rentenmark”. Yet comparatively little was needed for it after so much had been done wrong for years.

The institutional lesson from this is now laid down in European treaty law. Article 123 TFEU (Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union) prohibits the ECB and the national central banks from financing states directly. Article 130 TFEU prohibits them from taking instructions from governments. Both provisions are the direct answer to the construction that was possible from 1914 to 1923.

bloecke.titel: Origins of the German fear of inflation
bloecke.md:
According to the common short version, 1923 destroyed people's savings, thereby made Germans receptive to extremists and is the reason why German monetary policy is strict to this day. The first and last parts are true; the middle one falls short.

The Hitler Putsch of 8/9 November 1923 did fall in the final phase of the inflation, but it failed. The NSDAP (Nazi Party) only became strong seven years later, and under the opposite conditions, namely deflation, austerity and mass unemployment. In Germany, the number of unemployed rose from around 1.9 million on average in 1929 to over 6 million in February 1932. The political catastrophe followed the deflation and not directly the hyperinflation.

The second experience is also mostly forgotten. In 1948, savers lost out again. In the currency reform, wages, rents and pensions were converted to Deutsche Marks at 1:1, while balances were initially converted at 10:1 and in the end at about 100 Reichsmarks to 6.50 Deutsche Marks. Twice within 25 years, monetary wealth in Germany was devalued, while tangible wealth was not. This explains the ingrained attitude better than 1923 alone.

Today, this attitude is mostly directed against securities and in favour of the instant-access savings account. It thus favours the form of wealth that disappeared completely in 1923 and avoids the form that, as a stake in real companies, at least had a core of substance.

In practice, the lower half of this table matters more. The consumer price index rose from 100 in 2020 to 125.8 in August 2026. A basket of goods that cost €100 back then now costs around €126, and a balance in a current account has lost around a fifth of its purchasing power in six years. This loss occurred gradually, without headlines and without any particular day on which it would have been noticed.

This yields the useful lesson for thinking in terms of tangible assets. A tangible asset protects you because its price rises with the price level over the long term, and only if you can hold it without being forced to sell. The fact that it is “real” is not sufficient reason. Property owners gained in 1923 mainly because their debts were wiped out. Rents did not contribute, because they were capped and lagged behind the depreciation. German shares did not offer reliable protection either. Calculated in gold or dollars, they lost a great deal of value at times during the inflation and only caught up after the stabilisation. Investors who had to sell at the wrong moment therefore lost out even with the right asset.

“Debt is good when there is inflation.” This only applies to *unexpected* inflation. Expected inflation is already included in the interest rate, so a loan at 4% with expected inflation of 2% does not devalue itself. The bet only pays off if inflation turns out higher than expected; otherwise it costs money.

“The main thing is a tangible asset.” The leverage with which debtors won in 1923 became a burden in 1924, when loans once again cost real money. Investors who bet on a crisis with borrowed money therefore have to survive the stabilisation as well as the crisis.

“In an emergency, I'll move into foreign currency and gold.” The same state that devalues the currency can also regulate switching into other investments, and in 1923 foreign exchange transactions were placed under controls. A plan that is only to be put into action in an emergency is therefore not reliable.

For German practice in 2026, there is an additional point that played only a marginal role in 1923. Tax law makes no adjustment for inflation and taxes the nominal gain. Capital gains on securities are taxable under Section 20(2) EStG (Income Tax Act). The tax rate is 25% [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] under Section 32d(1) EStG, plus the solidarity surcharge and, where applicable, church tax. Only the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 under Section 20(9) EStG, or €2,000 for joint assessment, remains free of tax. For equity funds, the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] under Section 20(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act) reduces the tax base.

The situation is different for two classic tangible assets. The sale of physical gold is a private disposal transaction (privates Veräußerungsgeschäft) and is tax-free after a holding period of one year (Section 23(1) sentence 1 no. 2 EStG). If it is sold within the first year, an exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of €1,000 applies (Section 23(3) sentence 5 EStG). A buy-to-let property can be sold tax-free after ten years (Section 23(1) sentence 1 no. 1 EStG). This note is not a recommendation for gold or property. It shows that “tangible asset” is not a uniform concept for tax purposes.

bloecke.erklaerung: The net return is the return after tax on the nominal gain. Because the state also taxes the illusory gain, the real return falls as inflation rises, even if the pre-tax return stays the same in real terms.
variablen: nominal return after flat-rate withholding tax and surcharges
rise in the consumer price index over the same period
bloecke.beispiel: An equity ETF achieves a nominal return of 6% with inflation of 6%. The tax burden is 26.375% on 70% of the gain (partial exemption), that is, 18.5%, leaving 4.89% net. In real terms, this gives 1.0489 / 1.06 − 1 = −1.0%. In nominal terms there is a gain, in real terms a loss.

bloecke.md:
- Protection against inflation comes from a broad stake in real productive assets over long periods. Reallocating at the moment when the inflation rate is in the news does not achieve this.
- A mortgage loan with a long fixed-rate period is today's equivalent of the 1923 inflation bet. It is only sustainable if the instalment and income still match even if inflation fails to materialise.
- Wealth held entirely in one currency and one legal jurisdiction depends wholly on how they develop. Diversifying across several currency areas is a prudent way of putting the tangible asset idea into practice.

mitnehmen: The factor of one trillion in nine years became visible in 1923, but its cause lies in the decision of 1914 to have government spending permanently financed by the country's own central bank.

Whether a currency collapses depends on the velocity of money as well as on the money supply, because as soon as everyone spends their money immediately, the flight from money accelerates the decline.
The inflation redistributed wealth from creditors to debtors; the biggest winner was the state, and those worst off were the subscribers to war bonds.
The Rentenmark had no redeemable backing; the inflation was ended by a credible limit on the money supply, which today is safeguarded by Articles 123 and 130 TFEU.

The inflation risk in Germany today lies less in a hyperinflation than in the gradual loss of around a fifth of purchasing power between 2020 and 2026, which the taxation of nominal gains makes even worse.

begriffe.text: Extreme currency depreciation, usually from a price rise of about 50% a month. More important than the level of the rate is the collapse of the functions of money. Money first loses its function as a store of value, then as a unit of account and finally as a means of payment.

Transitional currency introduced on 15 November 1923 that, from 20 November, was equivalent to 1 trillion paper marks. It was nominally backed by land charges on agriculture, industry and trade, but it was not redeemable. What stabilised it were the fixed limit on its quantity and the end of central bank loans to the Reich.

Measure of how often a unit of money is used for purchases in a given period; the V in the equation of exchange M × V = P × Y. In hyperinflations it rises sharply because nobody wants to hold money, and prices then rise faster than the money supply.

Nominal increase in value that merely reflects inflation and creates no purchasing power in real terms. German tax law does not adjust capital income for inflation and therefore taxes illusory gains as well.

Asset whose price rises with the price level over the long term, such as productive assets, property or commodities. The protection against inflation only applies over long periods and only for owners who are not forced to sell.
